title: Micro-organisms and Immunity
seo_title: Grade 8 Science: Micro-organisms and Immunity Worksheets (BC Curriculum)
standard_text: Micro-organisms can be helpful or harmful: bacteria, viruses and fungi, how diseases spread, the body's defences and the immune system, vaccination, antibiotics, and epidemics. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Science 8, Biology)
meta_desc: Free Grade 8 science worksheets (BC): bacteria, viruses and fungi, infectious diseases, the immune system, vaccines and antibiotics. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Vaccines train the body; antibiotics kill bacteria.
body_html:
How to think about it

Micro-organisms include bacteria, fungi, protists and viruses. Many are helpful (yeast in bread, bacteria in yogurt and in our gut), but some are pathogens that cause disease. Diseases spread by droplets, touch, food and water, and animal bites.

The body's first defences are skin, mucus and stomach acid. White blood cells attack pathogens and make antibodies. A vaccine trains the immune system before infection. Antibiotics kill bacteria but do not work on viruses.

Example

Will antibiotics cure a cold?

Colds are caused by viruses.

Answer: no

Example

How does a vaccine protect you?

It is a harmless version or part of a pathogen.

Answer: it trains the immune system to make antibodies

Common mistakes

  • Thinking antibiotics kill viruses.
  • Thinking all bacteria are harmful.
  • Not finishing a course of antibiotics.

items.q: How do hairs and mucus in the nose help defend the body?
c: They trap particles that may contain pathogens.
They move mucus with trapped pathogens up to the throat.
It kills pathogens in food and drink.
They attach to antigens on pathogens so they can be destroyed.
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: What is a pathogen?
c: a type of white blood cell
items.e: Viruses, bacteria, fungi, protists.

items.q: What is herd immunity?
c: When most people are vaccinated, the disease cannot spread easily, protecting those who are not immune.
items.e: This protects babies and people who cannot be vaccinated.

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Kills pathogens in food and drink”?
c: hairs and mucus in the nose
cilia in the trachea and bronchi
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.q: What is an antigen?
c: a molecule on the surface of a pathogen that triggers the making of antibodies
a type of white blood cell
items.e: Each pathogen has its own antigens.

items.q: Why should a patient finish the whole course of antibiotics?
c: to kill all the bacteria, so resistant ones are less likely to survive and multiply
items.e: Stopping early can leave the toughest bacteria alive.

items.q: How do cilia in the trachea and bronchi help defend the body?

items.q: How do bacteria make us ill?
c: They reproduce quickly and may make toxins that damage tissues.
items.e: Toxins.

items.q: Why does a vaccinated person not become ill when infected?
c: The vaccine stays in the blood for ever as antibodies.
The vaccine kills all pathogens in the air.
Memory cells make antibodies quickly, before the pathogen can multiply.
items.e: The secondary response is faster and larger.

items.q: Which part of the body's defences does this: “Engulf and digest pathogens”?
items.e: First and second lines of defence.

items.e: This is natural selection.

items.q: Which cells make antibodies?
items.e: Phagocytes engulf pathogens.

items.q: Why must a new influenza vaccine be made each year?
c: The virus mutates, so its antigens change.
The old vaccine stops working in the fridge.
items.e: Memory cells may not recognize the new antigens.

items.q: What type of pathogen causes the common cold?
items.e: Antibiotics can treat bacterial diseases, but not viral ones.

items.q: A health worker is injected with ready-made antibodies after a needle-stick injury. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: Can the common cold be treated with antibiotics?
c: only if a vaccine is also given
items.e: The common cold is caused by a virus. Antibiotics kill bacteria but have no effect on viruses.

items.q: A patient with a dangerous infection is given a serum of antibodies from a donor. Which type of immunity is this?
items.e: Active: the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells (long-lasting). Passive: ready-made antibodies are given (short-lived).

items.q: Which is one way antibodies help to destroy pathogens? They…

turn the pathogen into a vaccine
items.e: Antibodies are proteins made by lymphocytes. They neutralize toxins made by bacteria, among other actions.

items.q: Why does euglena have both a chloroplast and an eyespot?
c: It is a plant cell only.
It can make food in light and swims towards light.
items.e: A unicellular organism.

items.q: A slice of potato is placed in very salty water. What happens?
c: Water leaves the potato cells by osmosis, so the slice becomes soft and limp.
The potato gains water and swells.
items.e: Water moves to the saltier side.

items.q: An amoeba is a single cell. Why does it not need a transport system?
c: It has a large surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion is fast enough.
items.e: Substances only need to travel a short distance.

items.q: Why are farmers told not to over-fertilize? Too much fertilizer in the soil can
c: make the soil water more concentrated than the cell sap, so water leaves the roots by osmosis
items.e: The plants may wilt.

items.q: What is an amoeba?
c: a unicellular organism that moves and feeds by changing shape
items.e: One cell does everything.

items.q: Which describes a capillary?
c: It has no wall at all.
It has a thinner wall and valves to stop blood flowing backwards.
It has a thick, muscular, elastic wall to withstand high pressure.
It has a wall only one cell thick.
items.e: A capillary has a wall only one cell thick.

items.q: A student puts a balsam plant in red-coloured water. After a day, she cuts across the stem. Where is the red colour?
items.e: Xylem carries water up the stem.

items.q: Why does the blood in an artery spurt out when it is cut, but blood in a vein flows out slowly?
c: Blood in arteries is under much higher pressure.
items.e: Arteries carry blood pumped by the heart.

items.q: Why do the lungs have a huge surface area?
c: so lots of oxygen can diffuse into the blood quickly
items.e: Bigger surface, faster diffusion.

items.q: A person's capillaries are damaged. Which process is most affected?
c: the exchange of oxygen and food with body cells
items.e: Exchange happens across capillary walls.

items.q: Why do plants wilt if their roots are damaged?
c: Less water can be absorbed and carried up the xylem.
The leaves make too much food.
The phloem carries too much water.
items.e: Water keeps cells firm.

items.q: Why does diffusion happen faster when it is warmer?
items.e: Temperature affects diffusion.

items.q: Why do cells divide?
c: for growth, repair and to replace old cells
items.e: Skin cells are replaced every few weeks.

items.q: Why do wilted celery sticks become firm in fresh water?
c: Water enters the cells by osmosis and fills the vacuoles.
The celery grows new cells in minutes.
items.e: Turgor keeps plants firm.

items.q: Which blood vessel carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells?
items.e: A capillary carries blood through the tissues, where substances are exchanged with the cells.

items.q: Which blood vessel has a thinner wall and valves to stop blood flowing backwards?
items.e: A vein has a thinner wall and valves to stop blood flowing backwards.

items.q: A student drew a cheek cell with a cell wall. What mistake did she make?
c: Cheek cells have no cell membrane.
Animal cells do not have a cell wall.
items.e: Only plant cells have a cell wall.

items.q: Which describes a vein?
c: It has no wall at all.
It has a thinner wall and valves to stop blood flowing backwards.
It has a thick, muscular, elastic wall to withstand high pressure.
It has a wall only one cell thick.
items.e: A vein has a thinner wall and valves to stop blood flowing backwards.

items.q: Nathan looked at cheek cells and onion cells. Which part did he see only in the onion cells?
items.e: Cheek cells are animal cells.

items.q: What does 'selectively permeable' mean?
c: lets some substances through but not others
items.e: The cell membrane is selectively permeable.
